newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: I&J SEES THREAT TO S.AFRICA'S WILD ABALONE.
newsitem.headline: I&J SEES THREAT TO S.AFRICA'S WILD ABALONE.

text.p: South Africa's commercial wild abalone industry, worth about $14.8 million a year, could be destroyed in three or four years by poachers, food group Irvin & Johnson Ltd (I&J) said.
I&J's director of seafoods, Charles Atkins, said in an interview that uncontrolled poaching of the shellfish, highly sought after in Pacific Rim countries, was "a major threat".
He said poachers were estimated to remove 200 to 300 tonnes a year, compared with the 550 tonne total allowable catch granted to about 20 licensed operators this year.
"What is disturbing is that they are taking out undersized abalone, so these animals don't have a chance to spawn, so it's a net loss to the resource," Atkins said.

"It's the sort of resource that you will fish and the catch will be quite good right until the moment of collapse...so in the absence of knowledge of untouched resources, I would say in three to four years we may not have a commercial industry."
Abalone prices are volatile but Atkins said the current price was around $27 a kilo.
Fishermen along South Africa's south coast object to the present quota system, aimed at conserving abalone, on the grounds that it bars them from access to what they see as a common resource.
"You can't bring in everybody, the sea isn't big enough to accommodate everybody. There's always going to be disaffected people," Atkins said.
He said firms like I&J, which poachers accuse of monopolising the resource, were not given enough credit for having developed the market in abalone.
"It's a risk area and it's an area where we've invested a huge amount of time and effort and money in developing our market and our product," Atkins said.

He said South African production was small in world terms but its quality was highly regarded. "In the Chinese market we are the preferred specie after the Mexican. It's our particular texture, taste and mouth feel."
Atkins said I&J planned to begin selling farmed cocktail- size abalone on a commercial scale in December this year or January 1998.

"I think we've got a job to do in increasing distribution and consumption because there are a lot of people producing this kind of product -- Australia, Tasmania, New Zealand, United States, Taiwan, mainland China," he said.
I&J hoped to eventually produce 150 tonnes a year of farmed abalone, Atkins said.
He added that a successful launch depended on South Africa's major producers of farmed abalone marketing the product cooperatively.

"I can't see any kind of formalised one channel marketing, which is a great pity. In an infant industry you've got to do it. For I&J to have a head to head fight with Premier Ltd or Oceana Fishing Group Ltd , cut each other's throats, it's crazy," Atkins said.
